Ch10_1:101:
Answer: A. The stock rose in absolute terms but lagged a benchmark that rose faster.

Why: A relative strength (RS) line is simply the stock's price divided by the benchmark's price, here rebased so it starts at 100. In the top panel the price climbs from about 49.8 to about 59.8, a gain of roughly 20%. In the bottom panel the RS line slides from 100 to about 78. A falling ratio means the denominator (the benchmark) grew faster than the numerator (the stock). So the stock made money, but less than the index did.

Why not the others:
B – Outperformance would show as a rising RS line; this one falls by about 22%.
C – If the benchmark had fallen while the stock rose, the ratio would have risen sharply, not dropped.
D – An up-trending price only tells you about absolute performance; relative performance is read from the ratio, not the price.

Remember: The RS line answers "better or worse than the benchmark?", not "up or down?" — a stock can rise and still lose the race.
Ch10_1:102:
Answer: B. Sector B.

Why: A relative rotation graph (RRG) plots each sector's relative-strength ratio on the horizontal axis (100 = same as the benchmark) and the momentum of that ratio on the vertical axis (100 = neutral). The top-left box, IMPROVING, holds sectors whose ratio is still below 100 (still lagging overall) but whose momentum is above 100 (getting better). Sector B's latest large dot sits at about 97.9 on the ratio axis and about 102.2 on the momentum axis — left of 100 and above 100, so it is in IMPROVING. Its tail shows it climbed up out of the LAGGING box.

Why not the others:
A – Sector A sits near (104.8, 99.6): ratio above 100 but momentum below 100, which is WEAKENING.
C – Sector C sits near (95.8, 98.5): both coordinates below 100, which is LAGGING.
D – Sector D sits near (104.1, 103.0): both above 100, which is LEADING.

Remember: On an RRG, read the latest dot's x (trend) and y (momentum) against 100 — left-and-up is IMPROVING.
Ch10_1:103:
Answer: D. It still outperforms on relative trend, but its relative momentum has dropped below 100, so outperformance is losing steam.

Why: Sector A's latest dot is at a ratio of about 104.8 and momentum of about 99.6. The ratio above 100 means it is still beating the benchmark overall. The momentum just under 100 means the rate of that outperformance is slowing. Its tail shows the path: it came from the LEADING box (momentum above 103) and dropped straight down across the 100 line. Sectors usually rotate clockwise on an RRG, so WEAKENING often comes before LAGGING if the slide continues.

Why not the others:
A – The relative trend (x-axis) is about 104.8, still above the benchmark; only momentum fell below 100.
B – Starting new leadership would mean moving into LEADING, not out of it.
C – A came from LEADING, not LAGGING; the move from LAGGING into a better box would be into IMPROVING.

Remember: WEAKENING = still ahead of the benchmark, but the lead is shrinking — the typical next stop is LAGGING.
Ch10_1:104:

Meanwhile the price in the top panel is about 58.6, still under its prior high of 60. So the stock is beating the index even though it has not yet beaten its own old high. When relative strength breaks out first, it shows money is favouring the stock, and price often follows with its own breakout.

Why not the others:
B – Underperformance would show as a falling RS line; this one is at new highs.
C – A new RS high with price lagging is a positive lead, not a bearish divergence; bearish divergence is price up while RS fails.
D – Price is below its prior 60 high; only the ratio made a new high.

Remember: An RS line that breaks out before price is an early vote of leadership.

B – 5.0% is just Q's return minus the index return (15% − 10%); the ratio change is 1.15 ÷ 1.10 − 1 ≈ 4.5%.
D – 12.5% is P's own price change, ignoring the index entirely.

Ch11_1:101:
Answer: A. Right translation; the longer trend is bullish.

Why: Translation describes where a cycle's peak falls compared with the midpoint between its two troughs. On this 40-bar cycle the midpoint is bar 20 (dashed line), but price keeps rising past it and peaks near bar 29 at about 22.3, before falling to about 16 at bar 40. A peak shifted to the right of the midpoint is called right translation. It means price spent more of the cycle rising than falling, which usually happens when a longer, larger cycle is pushing prices up. Note also that the ending trough (about 16) is above the starting trough (10), another sign of an uptrend.

Why not the others:
B – Left translation is a peak before the midpoint; this peak is after it.
C – The label is right, but right translation points to a bullish, not bearish, longer trend.
D – Left translation is the wrong label and it usually goes with a bearish longer trend.

Remember: Peak to the Right = Rising longer trend; peak to the Left = Lower longer trend.

T4→T5 = 146 − 112 = 34 bars

Next trough T6 ≈ T5 + average = 146 + 34 = bar 180. In practice you treat this as a window around bar 180, not an exact day.

B – Bar 173 uses too short a period (27 bars), shorter than any completed cycle on the chart.
D – Bar 214 adds about two full cycles to T5, skipping the next trough.

B – Cycle 1 (blue) has the larger amplitude, not Cycle 2, and the deepest lows need both cycles low.
D – When Cycle 2 peaks while Cycle 1 bottoms, they offset each other, giving a shallower low.

Remember: Summation — cycles add up, so the biggest lows come when several cycles bottom at once.
Ch11_1:104:

Why not the others:
A – Two is the A-to-B ratio (80 ÷ 40), not A-to-C.
B – The count is right, but proportionality links a cycle's amplitude to its period, not the period ratio.
C – Eight would need a 10-bar Cycle C; nominality is about a common set of cycle lengths, not this ratio.

Remember: Harmonicity — neighbouring cycles are usually 2× (sometimes 3×) each other.

Ch11_2:103:

C – An exponent below 0.5 means anti-persistence, and Q is the trending series.
D – An exponent above 0.5 means moves tend to continue, which suits trend-following, not mean-reversion.

Remember: H > 0.5 trends (follow it); H < 0.5 reverts (fade it); H = 0.5 is random.

B – A very high in-sample Sharpe with a collapse out of sample is the signature of overfitting, not robustness.
C – Some drop out of sample is normal; Y's small decline (1.30 to 1.15) is a good result.
D – A low in-sample figure does not prevent curve-fitting, and Z still lost almost half its edge.

Why: A W-bottom is a double bottom read relative to the Bollinger Bands, not just raw prices. At low 1 (around bar 27) price falls to about 61.1, below the lower band (about 62): sellers are very strong. Price then bounces to about 69.8 (around bar 35). At low 2 (around bar 47) price falls slightly lower, to about 60.6, but now sits well inside the lower band (about 58.7). So, relative to volatility, the second low is weaker selling: a higher low in band terms. The pattern is confirmed when price rallies above the intervening high of about 69.8, which it does around bar 55, reaching about 71.7.

Why not the others:
B – A lower price low inside the band shows weaker selling, not a continuing breakdown.
C – In a Bollinger W-bottom the second low may be slightly lower in price; what matters is that it holds inside the band.
D – A double top forms at highs; this pattern forms at lows.

Remember: W-bottom = first low outside the lower band, second low inside it, confirmed by a break above the middle peak.
